newsitem.title: GERMANY: Are money supply targets right for the ECB?.
newsitem.headline: Are money supply targets right for the ECB?.

text.p: As Dutchman Wim Duisenberg prepares to take the helm at the European Monetary Institute next week, economists are zeroing in on how European monetary policy should best be steered to protect the future euro.

The EMI, which will become the European Central Bank in 1998, has suggested interest rates should be set in relation to either money supply or inflation targets, but has left it up to the ECB itself to make the final decision.
Although a final decision lies in the future, lobby groups are already forming to press their point and economists are engaged in a heated debate over which instrument should be crowned the winner.

For some, money supply, favoured by the Bundesbank, is simply not a reliable or transparent enough indicator to inspire the confidence of financial markets or the public that inflation will be kept under control.
"I would come down firmly in favour of inflation targeting," said Brian Venables, senior bond stategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.

"Historically M3 was a very good indicator of future inflation because of the capital controls that reasonably closed economies enforced. But with the advent of European integration and disbanding of capital controls, M3 no longer offers any viable indication of future inflationary pressure."
The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said earlier this month that a direct inflation target would be more reliable as an ECB policy guide.

And money supply targeting -- which in Germany focuses on traditional M3, including cash in circulation, time, sight and short-term savings deposits -- has also been largely abandoned by many other European countries.

Analysts say a decline in capital controls, changes in investors' saving patterns and growth in financial market transactions not counted in M3, have in the last few years sparked sizeable fluctuations and distortions in the data.
These movements have prompted many central banks to jump ship and switch to inflation targeting for monetary policy.

Even though it has hit its annual target only once in the past five years, the Bundesbank continues to set a yearly M3 growth target zone, saying monetary policy aimed at harnessing inflation will be steered with this zone in mind.

The Bundesbank also defends the indicator for Europe, arguing the long-term link between current money supply growth rates and future inflation is still valid and that in the longer term money supply data will restabilise.

"Initial studies have confirmed that the long-term stability of money demand in the euro currency area should give the necessary basis for a money supply strategy," Europe's most powerful central bank said in its 1996 report.
Bronwyn Curtis, chief economist at Nomura International in London, said while recent fluctuations in M3 mean the indicator has been somewhat discredited, it remains a useful tool.

"If you're not going to use money supply, you have to have a range of other indicators -- most economists would look at output, try to measure output gaps, look at producer prices, and so on. But those methods are a bit more 'seat of the pants'," she said.
"The Bundesbank still sets an M3 target, still looks at it, and is still the most successful of all the central banks in terms of controlling inflation."

But while the Bundesbank enjoys an enviable reputation for controlling price pressures, the future ECB will have no past to back it up, and an urgent need to pacify financial markets and the European public with a firm hand on inflation.
Against this backdrop, some analysts say M3 targets are unlikely to be of much use.

"It is debatable whether the experience gathered by the Bundesbank can simply be transferred to the ECB, which has no track record," Peter Cornelius, head of international economics at Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt, said in a recent study.

Cornelius said the introduction of the euro, scheduled for January 1999, may prompt further fundamental changes in behaviour -- for example, more centralised corporate treasury functions or more widespread consumer credit card use.
These changes, if they were to come about, would make predicting money demand yet more difficult, he said.

"In light of these uncertainties, we see a major advantage in a monetary policy based on explicit inflation targets," Cornelius said. "Since inflation targeting enjoys a greater degree of flexibility to react with respect to unforeseen developments, a central bank without a track record may find it easier to establish and maintain credibility."

In the eyes of the general public too, ABN Amro's Venables said an inflation target is clearer, easier to measure performance against and would therefore ease the ECB's quest for support and credibility.

"Everyone in the public understands the notion of inflation. But money supply -- even the definition of what constitutues money supply -- I don't think is something that the average layman fully understands."
